texts.text: The community pool will close at four o'clock on Saturday for scheduled maintenance of the filtration system. Swimmers are asked to collect any belongings from the lockers before then, because the changing rooms will be cleaned overnight. Lessons planned for Sunday morning will go ahead as usual, and the café will stay open until six. Thank you for your patience while the work is completed.

Rinse one cup of red lentils until the water runs clear. Warm two tablespoons of oil in a heavy pot, add a chopped onion, and cook it slowly until soft and golden. Stir in garlic, cumin, and a pinch of chili, then add the lentils with four cups of stock. Simmer for twenty minutes, season with lemon juice and salt, and serve with warm flatbread.

Hi Priya, thanks for sending the draft schedule so quickly. I looked through it last night and the only conflict I can see is the Thursday afternoon slot, which overlaps with the supplier visit. Could we move the design review to Friday morning instead? Everything else works for me. I will bring the printed floor plans and the revised budget to the meeting.

07:40 — light rain, wind from the northwest at roughly 15 km/h. Two herons on the eastern bank, one juvenile. The water level at the gauge reads 1.32 m, about 8 cm higher than Tuesday. Mud on the lower path is deep enough to slow the wheelbarrow. Counted 23 coots near the reeds and a single kingfisher that flew upstream before I could note the band colour.

I bought this kettle after my old one started leaking from the base. It boils a full litre in a little under three minutes and the switch clicks off reliably. The handle stays cool, which matters with small children around. My only complaint is the lid, which is stiff to open with one hand. For the price it does exactly what I need, and the limescale filter is easy to remove and rinse.

When the canal opened in 1828, the town at its western end grew faster than anyone had planned. Warehouses appeared along the wharf within a decade, and the population doubled as families arrived to work the barges and the new brick kilns. The old market square, built for a village, could no longer cope with the traffic of carts and livestock. In 1841 the council bought a field beyond the church and laid out a second market with covered stalls and a weighing house. Most of those buildings have since been demolished, but the weighing house survives as a small museum, and its iron scales are still balanced every spring by volunteers who keep the original ledgers.

The service writes each incoming event to an append-only log before acknowledging it. A background worker reads the log in batches of up to five hundred records, validates them against the schema, and forwards valid records to the analytics store. Invalid records are moved to a quarantine table together with the validation error so that an operator can inspect them later. If the worker crashes, it resumes from the last committed offset, which means some records may be processed twice; the analytics store therefore deduplicates on the event identifier. Retention for the raw log is fourteen days, after which segments are compressed and archived to cold storage.

'You said the train left at nine,' Elena said, staring at the empty platform. 'I said it usually leaves at nine,' her brother replied. 'That is a different sentence.' She sat down on the bench and pulled her scarf tighter. 'Usually is doing a lot of work there.' He checked the timetable again, then the clock, then the timetable. 'There is another one at ten fifteen. We could get breakfast.' 'With what money? You spent the last of it on that umbrella.' He opened the umbrella, which was bright yellow and far too large, and held it over both of them although it was not raining. After a while she laughed, and they went to look for the café.

Plants lose water through tiny pores on their leaves called stomata. Each pore is surrounded by two guard cells that swell or shrink depending on how much water they hold. When the guard cells are full, they bend apart and the pore opens, letting carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis and letting water vapour escape. On hot, dry days many plants partly close their stomata to save water, even though this slows their growth. Scientists measure this trade-off to understand how crops might respond to longer droughts, and some breeding programmes now select varieties whose stomata respond more quickly to changes in light and humidity.

Dear Mr Okafor, I am writing to thank you for the time you spent with our students during last week's visit to the printing works. Many of them had never seen a press in operation, and your explanation of how the plates are prepared made the whole process easy to follow. Several students have since asked whether they could return for a longer project in the summer term. If that would be possible, I would be glad to discuss dates and any safety requirements with you. Please also pass on our thanks to your colleagues in the bindery, who answered a great many questions with remarkable patience. With kind regards, Helen Marsh, Year Ten coordinator.

The road to the monastery climbs for nearly eleven kilometres, switching back and forth across a slope of pale limestone and stunted pines. We set out before sunrise to avoid the heat, carrying more water than seemed sensible, and were grateful for every bottle by the halfway point. Goats watched us from ledges that looked impossible to reach. Around the seventh bend the trees thinned and the whole valley opened below us: terraced fields, a river the colour of tea, and the faint grey line of the coastal highway far to the south. The monastery itself appears suddenly, built into a fold of the cliff so that its walls seem to grow from the rock. A single monk was sweeping the courtyard when we arrived. He nodded, pointed us toward a stone basin of cold spring water, and went back to his sweeping without a word. Inside, the chapel was dark and cool and smelled of beeswax. Frescoes covered every surface, many of them faded to ghosts of red and ochre, but a few panels near the altar had been restored and glowed with a startling blue. We stayed until the light shifted and the paintings sank back into shadow, then began the long walk down.

Section 4. Remote work. Employees may work from a location other than the office for up to three days in any calendar week, subject to the approval of their line manager. Approval should not be withheld without a documented operational reason. Employees working remotely must remain reachable during core hours, which are ten o'clock to three o'clock local time, and must attend any meeting scheduled at least forty-eight hours in advance either in person or by video. Equipment supplied by the company remains company property and must be returned within ten working days of the end of employment. Employees are responsible for ensuring that their remote workspace meets the health and safety guidance published on the intranet, and may request an ergonomic assessment once in any twelve-month period. Confidential documents must not be printed at home. Breaches of this section will be handled under the standard disciplinary procedure, and repeated breaches may result in the withdrawal of remote-work approval for a period decided by the department head.

A late header from the substitute defender rescued a point for the visitors on Saturday after a match that had seemed to be slipping away from them for most of the second half. The home side started brightly, pressing high and forcing three corners in the opening ten minutes, and took the lead when their captain curled a free kick over the wall and in off the post. The visitors struggled to string passes together until just before half-time, when a quick exchange down the left produced their first shot on target. After the break the pattern continued: the hosts controlled possession, hit the crossbar twice, and should have been out of sight by the hour mark. Instead, a slack clearance in stoppage time fell to the visiting winger, whose cross was met at the far post by a player who had been on the pitch for less than five minutes. The home manager described the result as a lesson in finishing. His opposite number simply said that his team had refused to stop running.

Before you begin, switch off the power to the circuit at the consumer unit and confirm with a voltage tester that the old fitting is dead. Unscrew the ceiling rose cover and take a photograph of the existing wiring so you can refer to it later. Loosen the terminal screws and remove the wires one at a time, labelling each with masking tape. Feed the wires through the mounting plate of the new fitting and fix the plate to the ceiling using the screws provided, making sure they bite into a joist or a suitable cavity fixing. Connect the earth wire first, then the neutral, then the live, following the colour codes in the manufacturer's diagram rather than the colours you remember from older installations. Tighten every terminal firmly and tug gently on each wire to check it is held. Fit the shade or diffuser, restore the power, and test the switch. If the light flickers or the breaker trips, switch off again and check each connection before trying a second time. When in doubt, consult a qualified electrician.

Libraries are often described as quiet places, but the quiet is the least interesting thing about them. What matters is the kind of attention they make possible. In a library, a person can follow a question without being asked to buy anything, explain themselves, or produce a result by the end of the afternoon. That freedom is rarer than it looks. Most public spaces now expect something in return for the time spent in them, whether it is a purchase, a click, or a measurable outcome. The library asks only that you return the books. Critics sometimes argue that search engines have made libraries obsolete, since almost any fact can be found in seconds. But a fact is not the same as understanding, and a list of results is not the same as a shelf. Browsing a shelf exposes you to the neighbours of the book you came for, and those neighbours are chosen by a classification system rather than by a prediction of what you already like. The accident of proximity is a quiet engine of discovery. Libraries also hold things that are inconvenient to digitise: local newspapers, parish records, the photographs of a town that no longer looks the way it did. Losing them would not make the world faster; it would make it thinner.

The lighthouse had been automated for twenty years, but Ansel still climbed the stairs every evening at dusk. Nobody paid him to do it. The coastguard had written twice to explain that the lamp no longer needed a keeper, and the second letter had been less polite than the first. He kept both letters in a drawer with his father's compass and a tin of buttons whose purpose he had forgotten. The stairs numbered one hundred and twelve. He counted them aloud, not because he was afraid of losing track but because the counting gave the climb a shape, and a shape was easier to carry than a habit. At the top he wiped the salt from the inside of the glass with a cloth, checked the log that nobody read, and stood for a while watching the beam sweep the water. On clear nights he could see the lights of the fishing fleet strung along the horizon like a necklace. On foggy nights he saw nothing at all, and those were the nights he liked best, because the beam turned through the white and lit up nothing but itself, and he felt that someone ought to be there to witness it. One autumn a girl from the village began to follow him. She said she was writing a school project on the history of the coast, but she asked no questions about history. She wanted to know how the lens was cleaned, what the different flashes meant, and whether the light ever went wrong. He told her the truth: that it almost never did, and that when it did, a computer in a city two hundred miles away noticed before he could. She considered this for a long time. Then she asked why he came, if the computer noticed first. He found he had no answer that would fit inside a school project. He told her instead about the night the generator failed during a storm, before the automation, when his father had kept the lamp turning by hand for six hours while the waves broke over the gallery rail. She wrote everything down. The next evening she came again, and the evening after that, and by the end of the winter she was counting the stairs out loud with him, one hundred and twelve, and wiping the salt from the glass on the side he could no longer reach. In the spring the coastguard wrote a third time. The letter said that the lighthouse would be sold, that the new owners intended to turn it into holiday flats, and that access to the tower would end on the first of June. Ansel read it twice and put it in the drawer with the others. On the last evening the girl brought a flask of tea and a camera, and they climbed together, counting, and stayed at the top until the beam had swept the dark water a thousand times.

Minutes of the Allotment Committee, held in the pavilion on the third Tuesday of March. Present: the chair, the treasurer, the secretary, and nine plot holders. Apologies were received from two members. Item one: the minutes of the February meeting were approved without amendment. Item two: the treasurer reported a balance of four thousand two hundred and sixty pounds, of which nine hundred pounds is committed to the replacement of the water tank by the south gate. Rent payments are up to date for all but three plots, and reminders have been sent. Item three: the chair raised the issue of bonfires. After discussion, the committee agreed that bonfires will be permitted only between November and February, only after four in the afternoon, and only when the wind is blowing away from the houses on Mill Lane. The secretary will update the noticeboard. Item four: a proposal to create a shared wildlife area on the vacant plot near the hedge was welcomed. Two volunteers offered to draw up a planting plan using native species and to report back in April. Concerns were raised about rabbits, and the committee agreed that fencing should be included in the costs. Item five: the annual seed swap will take place on the first Saturday of April from ten until one. Members are encouraged to bring labelled packets and to avoid bringing seeds from plants that showed signs of blight last season. Item six: any other business. A plot holder reported that the combination lock on the tool shed has become difficult to open in cold weather. The secretary will ask the supplier for advice and, if necessary, purchase a replacement. Another member asked whether the committee would consider installing a second compost bay, as the existing bays fill up quickly in autumn. The treasurer agreed to obtain quotations. There being no further business, the meeting closed at half past eight. The next meeting will be held on the third Tuesday of April at seven o'clock, and all plot holders are welcome to attend.

The common swift is a medium-sized bird that spends almost its entire life in the air. Adults land only to nest, and young birds that leave the nest may remain airborne for two or three years before breeding for the first time. Swifts feed on flying insects and airborne spiders, which they catch in their wide gape while flying with mouths open, and they drink by skimming the surface of lakes and rivers. They sleep on the wing at high altitude, gliding in slow circles and descending gradually through the night. Their long, sickle-shaped wings and short forked tails make them well adapted to sustained flight, but their legs are short and weak, so a swift grounded on flat land can struggle to take off again. In Europe, swifts are among the latest migrants to arrive in spring and among the earliest to leave in late summer, spending the northern winter in sub-Saharan Africa. Their numbers have fallen sharply in many countries over recent decades. Researchers point to two main causes: a decline in insect populations and the loss of nesting sites, since swifts traditionally nest in gaps under roof tiles and in the eaves of older buildings, many of which have been renovated or sealed. Conservation groups now encourage the installation of purpose-built swift bricks and nest boxes on new and existing buildings, and some towns run volunteer surveys to map colonies so that they can be protected during construction work. Swifts are long-lived for their size; individuals ringed as adults have been recaptured more than eighteen years later, which means a single bird may fly several million kilometres over its lifetime. They pair for life and usually return to the same nest site each year. Both parents incubate the eggs and feed the young, carrying food in a ball of insects held together with saliva, called a bolus, that can contain more than a thousand individual insects. During spells of cold, wet weather, when insects are scarce, nestlings can enter a state of torpor, lowering their body temperature and surviving for several days without food until their parents return.

Residents of the northern districts were advised to boil drinking water on Wednesday after routine testing detected bacteria at a pumping station that serves about forty thousand homes. The water utility said the contamination was identified during a scheduled inspection and that there was no evidence anyone had fallen ill. Engineers isolated the affected station within two hours and began flushing the network with chlorinated water from a neighbouring supply. A spokesperson said the boil notice would remain in place until two consecutive sets of samples, taken twenty-four hours apart, came back clear. Bottled water distribution points were opened at three schools and a sports centre, and the utility said it would deliver water directly to residents registered as vulnerable, including those receiving home dialysis. Local businesses reacted with frustration. Several cafés closed for the day, and a bakery owner said she had thrown away the morning's dough because she could not be certain which batch of water had been used. The council's health committee called an emergency meeting for Thursday evening and asked the utility to present a full timeline of the incident, including when the bacteria were first detected and how quickly residents were informed. Some residents said they had learned about the notice from social media before receiving any official message. The utility acknowledged that its text-alert system had reached only around sixty per cent of registered customers on the first attempt and said it was investigating the cause. An independent water quality regulator confirmed it had been notified and would review the utility's response. Similar incidents in other regions in recent years have been traced to damaged pipes, flooding near treatment works, and failures in disinfection equipment. Engineers said it was too early to say what had caused the latest contamination but that the station's ultraviolet treatment unit would be examined as a priority. Residents are advised to boil water for at least one minute and let it cool before drinking it, brushing teeth, or preparing food. Water used for washing and bathing does not need to be boiled, although parents are advised to take care that young children do not swallow bath water. The utility has set up a dedicated helpline, which will remain staffed overnight. Councillors from the affected wards said they would press for compensation for households and businesses, pointing out that the same pumping station had been flagged for repairs in an inspection report two years ago. The utility declined to comment on the earlier report but said that a programme of upgrades across the northern network had been approved last autumn and was due to begin in the spring. Further updates will be published on its website every six hours until the notice is lifted.

The harbor town woke slowly on the first cold morning of autumn. Fishing boats knocked against the
pier while gulls argued over the remains of yesterday's catch. Mara walked the length of the seawall with her
hands in her pockets, counting the lamps that had failed overnight. There were seven, two more than last week,
and she wrote the numbers in a small notebook that had once belonged to her father. He had kept the lamps for
thirty years, climbing the iron ladders with a canvas bag of bulbs and fuses, and he had never once let the
whole wall go dark.

The council had promised new fixtures in the spring, then in the summer, and now nobody mentioned them at all.
Mara did not expect much from the council. She expected something from the ledger in the harbor office, where
every purchase since 1962 had been recorded in blue ink. If the bulbs could not be replaced, she wanted to know
where the money for them had gone. The office opened at nine. She had an hour, so she bought coffee from the
kiosk by the ferry ramp and sat on an upturned crate to watch the tide come in.

A ferry from the island arrived early, which was unusual. Most mornings it limped in twenty minutes late, its
engine coughing smoke the colour of wet slate. Today it glided to the ramp as if the sea had been rolled flat
for it. A handful of passengers stepped off: a woman with a cello case, two boys carrying a crate of apples
between them, and a tall man in a grey coat who paused at the bottom of the ramp and looked directly at the
broken lamps, one after another, as though he too were counting.

Mara watched him walk along the wall. He stopped beneath the fourth dead lamp, reached up, and tapped the iron
post twice with his knuckles. Then he took out a notebook of his own, wrote something, and moved on toward the
harbor office. She finished her coffee in one long swallow, which burned, and followed him at a distance that
she hoped looked casual.

The harbor office smelled of tar, paper, and the paraffin heater that had been running since before dawn. The
clerk, a young man named Tobias who had started in the spring, looked up with relief when the stranger came in,
as if he had been expecting him. They spoke quietly at the counter. Mara pretended to read the tide tables on the
wall and listened. The stranger was an engineer from the mainland, sent by the lighting company to survey the
seawall. The company, it seemed, had been paid for new fixtures eighteen months ago. Nobody at the company could
explain why the fixtures had never been installed, and nobody at the council had asked.
